definition: An authentication protocol for online card payments that adds a verification step (like a one-time code) to shift fraud liability from the merchant to the issuer.
When a fraudster gains access to a legitimate user's account through stolen credentials, phishing, or social engineering.
Card network services (Visa VAU, Mastercard ABU) that automatically update expired or replaced card credentials with merchants.
The department or process responsible for paying a company's bills and invoices to suppliers.
Automated Clearing House — the US system for batch bank-to-bank transfers, handling 82% of US electronic payments.
The bank or processor that handles card payments on behalf of the merchant.
A technology platform that routes transaction data from merchants through card networks for authorization and settlement.
Anti-Money Laundering — regulations requiring financial institutions to monitor transactions and report suspicious activity.
Networks like Plus (Visa), Cirrus (Mastercard), MoneyPass, and Allpoint that enable cross-bank ATM access.
A hold placed on funds at the time of a card swipe, dip, or tap. No money moves yet.
A temporary freeze on funds in the cardholder's account after an approved authorization. No money moves — the hold simply reserves the amount until clearing.
Address Verification Service — checks if the billing address provided matches the address on file with the card issuer.
Business-to-business payments — transactions between companies, typically larger amounts with more complex approval workflows.
Banking as a Service — the infrastructure stack that lets fintechs launch card programs without being banks.
Bankers' Automated Clearing Services — the UK system for direct debits and bank credits.
The practice of bundling a day's worth of approved transactions into a single file for submission to the acquirer — typically done at end of business day.
Bank Identification Number — the first six digits of a card number that identify the issuing bank.
A block of card numbers assigned to an issuer, used to generate virtual cards programmatically.
A simplified pricing model where merchants pay one flat rate regardless of card type — usually more expensive overall.
Buy Now, Pay Later — a financing option letting consumers split purchases into installments, typically interest-free.
A Brazilian payment method where consumers print a voucher and pay at banks, convenience stores, or via online banking.
The payment rail (like Visa or Mastercard) that connects issuers and acquirers and routes transactions between them.
A model where processors provide the full stack for issuing cards — from BIN sponsorship to processing — as a managed service.
A transaction where the card is not physically present — online purchases, phone orders, in-app payments.
A transaction where the physical card is present at the point of sale — chip dip, contactless tap, or magnetic stripe swipe.
A payment method where consumers pay in cash when goods are delivered — still common in emerging markets for e-commerce.
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — US agency overseeing consumer financial product regulation.
A forced reversal of a card transaction initiated by the cardholder's bank — pulling funds back from the merchant through the card network.
Cardholder-Initiated Transaction vs Merchant-Initiated Transaction — a Visa framework determining how recurring charges are classified.
The process where merchants confirm final transaction details and submit them to the card network — locking in amounts, tips, and adjustments before money moves.
A card network like American Express where a single company acts as issuer, acquirer, and network — controlling the entire transaction.
In card-not-present transactions, the merchant typically bears liability for fraud — unless additional authentication (like 3DS) shifts it to the issuer.
A card branded by both a retailer and a network (like Amazon Visa) — uses network rails but negotiates custom economics.
Pre-coded, modular components that can be assembled to create custom card programs without writing code from scratch.
A card program issued to a company's employees, with centralized billing and administrative controls.
A system where banks without direct relationships use intermediary banks to process international transfers.
The maximum amount a credit card issuer will lend you, checked during each authorization.
When a merchant's acquirer is in a different country than the transaction — resulting in higher fees and lower approval rates.
Card Verification Value — the 3-digit security code on the back of a card, proving the cardholder has the physical card.
Dynamic Currency Conversion — when a merchant offers to charge in the cardholder's home currency, usually at unfavorable exchange rates.
Decentralized Finance — financial services (lending, trading, payments) built on blockchain without traditional intermediaries.
A pull-based payment where the payee initiates the withdrawal from the payer's bank account.
US financial reform law enacted after the 2008 crisis, which includes the Durbin Amendment regulating debit interchange.
Device PAN — a token issued by the card network that replaces the actual card number on a specific device.
A transaction flow where authorization and clearing happen as two separate messages — typical of credit cards and signature-debit transactions.
US regulation capping debit interchange for banks with over $10 billion in assets at roughly 21 cents + 0.05%.
The chip card standard (Europay/Mastercard/Visa) that generates unique cryptograms per transaction, reducing fraud.
Since October 2015, if a merchant doesn't accept chip cards and fraud occurs, the merchant bears the liability instead of the issuer.
Enterprise Resource Planning — systems like SAP, Oracle, and NetSuite that manage business operations including accounts payable/receivable.
A legitimate transaction incorrectly blocked by fraud detection systems — often more costly than actual fraud.
The UK's real-time payment system, operational since 2008, processing payments in seconds 24/7.
Financial Action Task Force — the international body that sets global AML/KYC standards adopted by 200+ countries.
The Federal Reserve's instant payment service launched in 2023, competing with RTP to bring real-time payments to all US banks.
The Federal Reserve's real-time gross settlement system used by U.S. banks to transfer funds with immediate finality.
The standard card payment structure involving cardholder, merchant, issuing bank, and acquiring bank — with a card network connecting them in the middle.
When a legitimate cardholder disputes a charge they actually made — either due to confusion or intentional abuse of the chargeback system.
The debit card model — money must be in your account before you can spend it.
A permanent rejection of a transaction that cannot be retried — typically due to a closed account, stolen card, or invalid card number.
Ensuring a payment instruction can only be executed once, even if submitted multiple times — critical for preventing duplicate payments.
A fee paid by the merchant's bank (acquirer) to the cardholder's bank (issuer) on each card transaction.
A transparent pricing model where merchants pay the actual interchange fee plus a fixed processor markup.
Subscribers lost due to payment failures (expired card, insufficient funds) rather than deliberate cancellation.
Independent Sales Organization — a licensed reseller of merchant acquiring services.
The international standard messaging format used for card transaction communications — the language that every player in the payment chain speaks.
The bank that issued the card to the consumer and approves or declines transactions.
A technology company that handles transaction authorization, card management, and settlement on behalf of the issuing bank.
Installment plans offered by the card issuer (common in Latin America) where credit card purchases are automatically split into monthly payments.
Just-in-Time Funding — a model where cards hold $0 balance until a transaction occurs, funded in real-time.
Know Your Business — similar to KYC but for business entities, verifying company registration, ownership, and beneficial owners.
Know Your Customer — the process of verifying a customer's identity before allowing them to open accounts or transact.
The transfer of fraud liability from one party to another — EMV chip shifted card-present liability from merchants to issuers.
A layer-2 protocol on top of Bitcoin enabling near-instant, low-fee transactions for everyday payments.
When a merchant uses an acquirer in the same country — yielding better authorization rates and lower fees than cross-border acquiring.
Disbursing funds to sellers — via bank transfer, push-to-card, issued debit card, or wallet balance.
Mastercard's platform for pushing funds to Mastercard debit cards, originally developed as Omney.
Merchant Category Code — a four-digit code classifying the type of business, which affects interchange rates.
The entity listed as the seller in a transaction — the Merchant of Record bears primary liability for disputes and refunds.
BNPL offered at checkout by providers like Klarna or Affirm — the merchant pays a fee, the consumer pays in installments.
Mastercard Interface Processor — dedicated hardware connecting a processor to the Mastercard network (Banknet).
A US state-level license required to hold or transmit funds on behalf of others — a major compliance requirement for marketplaces.
Mail Order / Telephone Order — a card-not-present channel with its own interchange rates and fraud rules.
The organization governing ACH rules and file formats in the US.
A fee charged by the card network (Visa, Mastercard) on every transaction for operating the routing and settlement infrastructure.
Card networks issuing device-specific tokens (DPANs) so the real card number is never stored on a device or shared with merchants.
Near-Field Communication — the technology behind contactless 'tap to pay' using cards or mobile wallets.
Accounts banks hold with each other to facilitate cross-border transfers — 'nostro' (our account at your bank) and 'vostro' (your account at our bank).
Original Credit Transaction — the technical mechanism for push-to-card, essentially an in-store refund without an original purchase.
Originating Depository Financial Institution — the bank that initiates an ACH transaction on behalf of the sender.
Regulatory mandates (like PSD2) requiring banks to provide APIs for third-party access to account data and payment initiation.
Klarna's original model — buy now, receive an invoice, pay within 14-30 days.
A card network like Visa or Mastercard where the issuer and acquirer are separate banks, and any bank can participate.
A wallet like Apple Pay that stores card credentials and processes transactions over the underlying card network rails.
Payment Facilitator — a company that aggregates merchants under its own master merchant account, simplifying onboarding. Stripe and Square are prominent examples.
Software that captures card data from merchants (especially online) and passes it to the acquirer processor.
Dividing a single customer payment between multiple recipients — the platform's commission and the seller's share.
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — security requirements for any entity that stores or transmits card data.
When a debit card transaction is routed over PIN debit networks using PIN verification — typically lower interchange.
Secondary networks (like Interlink, Maestro, STAR) used for PIN-authenticated debit transactions with lower interchange.
Brazil's instant payment system launched in 2020 — free for consumers, available 24/7, adopted by 62% of Brazilians within a year.
An authorization for an estimated amount before the final charge is known — common at hotels, gas stations, and car rentals.
A store-branded card (like a Macy's card) that only works at that retailer — no network interchange applies.
The entity that manages day-to-day operations of a card program — compliance, customer service, vendor coordination.
Gradually requesting more identity verification as a user's transaction volume or risk level increases, rather than demanding everything upfront.
A temporary credit issued to the cardholder by their bank while a dispute is being investigated — the cardholder gets their money back immediately, before anyone determines who's at fault.
Payment Services Directive 2 — EU regulation requiring Strong Customer Authentication and mandating Open Banking APIs.
Payment Service Provider — a company that offers merchants the technology and services to accept payments, often bundling gateway, processing, and risk management.
A payment initiated by the sender that pushes funds to the recipient — the opposite of a pull payment like a card charge.
A payment method where users scan a QR code to initiate a payment — dominant in China and India via Alipay, WeChat Pay, and UPI.
A standardized code assigned to a chargeback by the card network that categorizes the dispute — such as fraud, merchandise not received, or duplicate processing.
Matching payment records to invoices and accounting entries — a major operational challenge in B2B payments.
US federal regulation protecting consumers in electronic fund transfers, including debit card transactions and ACH.
US federal regulation governing credit card disclosures, billing practices, and consumer dispute rights (Truth in Lending Act).
The process where a merchant challenges a chargeback by submitting evidence that the transaction was legitimate — literally 're-presenting' the charge.
The logic for re-attempting declined recurring payments — timing, frequency, and decay patterns matter significantly.
In ATM transactions, the issuing bank pays the ATM owner — the opposite of card purchase interchange.
Incentives funded by interchange revenue that credit card issuers offer to encourage card usage.
Real-Time Payments — The Clearing House's US instant payment network, push-only, available 24/7.
Strong Customer Authentication — PSD2 requirement for two-factor authentication on electronic payments in Europe.
The KYC/KYB process of verifying seller identity and legitimacy before allowing them to receive payments on a marketplace.
Single Euro Payments Area — the EU system for cross-border euro bank transfers across 36 countries.
The actual transfer of funds between financial institutions, calculated as net positions by the card network and executed through banking rails like Fedwire.
When a debit card transaction is routed over credit rails (Visa/MC) using signature verification instead of a PIN.
A transaction flow where authorization and clearing happen in one combined message — typical of PIN-debit transactions.
A virtual card that's valid for one transaction only, then automatically deactivated — maximizing security.
Self-executing code on a blockchain that automatically enforces agreement terms — the building block of DeFi.
A temporary rejection that may succeed if retried — often caused by insufficient funds, issuer timeouts, or temporary fraud flags.
Real-time rules on corporate cards — limiting spending by amount, merchant category, time, or geography per card.
A chartered bank that provides its banking license and BIN to enable fintechs to issue cards on card networks.
A cryptocurrency pegged to a fiat currency (like USDC or USDT) — designed to maintain stable value for payments use.
A wallet like PayPal that holds its own balance of funds, with users loading money in via bank transfer or card.
Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication — the messaging network banks use to communicate international wire transfer instructions.
Settlement that occurs one business day after the transaction. T+2 means two business days. 'T' stands for the transaction date.
A person with minimal credit history or identity documentation — common among immigrants, young adults, and the unbanked.
Replacing the actual card number with a unique token for each device or merchant, reducing data breach risk.
Receipt-level transaction detail (itemized line items) captured at point of sale — enables automatic receipt matching.
Unified Payments Interface — India's real-time payment system enabling instant bank-to-bank transfers via mobile, processing 12+ billion transactions monthly.
A fraud rule that flags or blocks transactions when too many occur in a short time period from the same card or account.
VisaNet Integrated Payment — Visa's connection infrastructure for processor integration.
A digital-only card number generated instantly, usable for online purchases or added to mobile wallets — no physical plastic needed.
Visa's platform for pushing funds directly to Visa debit cards and bank accounts in real time.
Subscribers who deliberately cancel their subscription.
Virtual Payment Address — the human-readable identifier used in UPI (like username@bank) instead of account numbers.
Card network policies protecting consumers from unauthorized transactions — the consumer isn't responsible for fraud on their card.
